title: Ensure TLS authentication for Docker daemon is configured
description: When the daemon listens on a TCP socket, anyone who can reach it controls the host unless TLS client verification is enabled. Compliant when no tcp:// host is configured, or when tlsverify, tlscacert, tlscert and tlskey are all set. The audit reads the running dockerd command line (ps) together with /etc/docker/daemon.json.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 2.8 Ensure TLS authentication for Docker daemon is configured

audit.command:
args=$(ps -eo args 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; s=$(printf '%s
' "$args" | grep '[d]ockerd'; cat /etc/docker/daemon.json 2>/dev/null); if printf '%s
' "$s" | grep -q 'tcp://'; then for k in tlsverify tlscacert tlscert tlskey; do printf '%s
' "$s" | grep -Eq -e "--$k|"$k"" || { echo "missing $k"; exit 0; }; done; fi; echo compliant

remediation.command: Configure "tlsverify": true, "tlscacert", "tlscert" and "tlskey" in /etc/docker/daemon.json (or the equivalent dockerd flags) for any tcp:// listener, or remove the TCP listener, then restart the Docker daemon.

title: Ensure that the Docker socket file ownership is set to root:docker
description: The Docker socket (anyone who can write it controls the daemon) must be owned by root:docker. The audit stats every existing candidate path (/var/run/docker.sock, /run/docker.sock); not applicable when none exists.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 3.15 Ensure that the Docker socket file ownership is set to root:docker

audit.command: for f in /var/run/docker.sock /run/docker.sock; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; o=$(stat -Lc '%U:%G' "$f") || exit 1; [ "$o" = root:docker ] || { echo "$f $o"; exit 0; }; done; echo compliant

remediation.command: for f in /var/run/docker.sock /run/docker.sock; do if [ -e "$f" ]; then chown root:docker "$f" || exit 1; fi; done

title: Ensure that the Docker socket file permissions are set to 660 or more restrictively
description: The Docker socket (anyone who can write it controls the daemon) must have mode 660 or more restrictive. The audit flags any existing candidate path (/var/run/docker.sock, /run/docker.sock) with permission bits outside 660; not applicable when none exists.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 3.16 Ensure that the Docker socket file permissions are set to 660 or more restrictively

audit.command: for f in /var/run/docker.sock /run/docker.sock; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; out=$(find "$f" -maxdepth 0 -perm /7117) || exit 1; [ -z "$out" ] || { echo "$f"; exit 0; }; done; echo compliant

remediation.command: for f in /var/run/docker.sock /run/docker.sock; do if [ -e "$f" ]; then chmod 660 "$f" || exit 1; fi; done

title: Ensure that privileged containers are not used
description: A privileged container gets all capabilities and device access and can trivially take over the host. Flags containers with HostConfig.Privileged true. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.5 Ensure that privileged containers are not used

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{.HostConfig.Privileged}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$2=="true" {print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Redeploy without --privileged (compose: remove 'privileged: true'); grant only specific capabilities or devices that are required.

title: Ensure that the Docker socket is not mounted inside any containers
description: A container with the Docker socket mounted can start privileged containers and fully control the host. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.32 Ensure that the Docker socket is not mounted inside any containers

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}}{{range .Mounts}} {{.Source}}{{end}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '/docker\.sock/{print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Redeploy without mounting /var/run/docker.sock; use a narrowly-scoped API proxy if a container genuinely needs Docker API access.

title: Ensure no running container is privileged
description: Privileged containers have nearly full host access.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark - Container runtime

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo 0; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.HostConfig.Privileged}}' $ids) || exit 1; printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -c true || true

remediation.command: Remove 'privileged: true' from the container/compose/Kubernetes spec and redeploy

title: Run the Docker daemon as a non-root user, if possible
description: Rootless mode executes the Docker daemon and containers inside a user namespace, with both the daemon and the container are running without root privileges. Rootless mode allows running the Docker daemon and containers as a non-root user to mitigate potential vulnerabilities in the daemon and the container runtime. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.

audit.command: Running the following command will show any running dockerd processes and which user that is managing the daemon. ps -fe | grep 'dockerd' Expected state: Follow the current Docker documentation on how to install the Docker daemon as a non-root user.

remediation.command: Follow the current Docker documentation on how to install the Docker daemon as a non-root user.

title: Ensure insecure registries are not used
description: Insecure registries are contacted without TLS verification, exposing image pulls to tampering. The audit lists the registry index configs that docker info reports as not secure (the default loopback CIDRs are not listed) and expects none.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 2.5 Ensure insecure registries are not used

audit.command: out=$(docker info --format '{{range .RegistryConfig.IndexConfigs}}{{if not .Secure}}{{.Name}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1; n=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -c . || true); echo "$n"

remediation.guidance: Remove entries from "insecure-registries" in /etc/docker/daemon.json (and --insecure-registry start-up flags), configure TLS on the registries, and restart the Docker daemon.

title: Ensure sensitive host system directories are not mounted on containers
description: Mounting host system directories (/, /boot, /dev, /etc, /lib, /proc, /sys, /usr) lets a container read or change the host. Flags those directories mounted in any mode, and anything below them mounted read-write. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.6 Ensure sensitive host system directories are not mounted on containers

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{range .Mounts}} {{.Source}}|{{.RW}}{{end}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '{for(i=2;i<=NF;i++){split($i,a,"|"); if(a[1] ~ /^\/(boot|dev|etc|lib|proc|sys|usr)?$/ || (a[2]=="true" && a[1] ~ /^\/(boot|dev|etc|lib|proc|sys|usr)\//)) print $1" "a[1]}}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Redeploy the container without bind mounts of sensitive host directories; if a file is truly needed, mount only that file read-only (-v /etc/foo:/etc/foo:ro).

title: Ensure the container host has been Hardened

title: Ensure that the version of Docker is up to date

An experienced attacker may be able to exploit known vulnerabilities resulting in them being able to attain inappropriate access ... title: Ensure network traffic is restricted between containers on the default bridge

remediation.guidance: Set "icc": false in /etc/docker/daemon.json (or start dockerd with --icc=false) and restart the Docker daemon; use user-defined networks and --link for containers that must communicate.

description: User namespace remapping maps root inside containers to an unprivileged host UID, limiting the impact of a container breakout. The audit checks that docker info lists name=userns under SecurityOptions.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 2.10 Enable user namespace support

audit.command: o=$(docker info --format '{{range .SecurityOptions}}{{.}} {{end}}') || exit 1; printf '%s\n' "$o" | grep -q 'name=userns' && echo compliant || echo missing

remediation.command: Ensure /etc/subuid and /etc/subgid contain a mapping, set "userns-remap": "default" in /etc/docker/daemon.json and restart the Docker daemon (existing images and volumes need to be re-created).

title: Ensure the default cgroup usage has been confirmed
description: The --cgroup-parent option allows you to set the default cgroup parent to use for all containers. If there is no specific usage requirement for this, the setting should be left at its default. System administrators typically define cgroups under which containers are supposed to run. Even if cgroups are not explicitly defined by the system administrators, containers run under docker cgroup by default. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 2.11 Ensure the default cgroup usage has been confirmed

audit.command: In order to confirm this setting, the dockerd start-up options and any settings in /etc/docker/daemon.json should be reviewed. To review the dockerd startup options, use: grep "--cgroup-parent" /etc/docker/daemon.json You should ensure that the --cgroup-parent parameter is either not set or is set as appropriate non-default cgroup. The contents of /etc/docker/daemon.json should also be checked for this setting.

remediation.command: The default setting is in line with good security practice and can be left in situ. If you wish to specifically set a non-default cgroup, pass the --cgroup-parent parameter to the Docker daemon when starting it. For example: dockerd --cgroup-parent=/foobar

title: Ensure that authorization for Docker client commands is enabled
description: An authorization plugin gives granular control over which Docker API commands each client may run. Compliant when --authorization-plugin or a non-empty "authorization-plugins" list is configured. The audit reads the running dockerd command line (ps) together with /etc/docker/daemon.json.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 2.13 Ensure that authorization for Docker client commands is enabled

audit.command: args=$(ps -eo args 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; s=$(printf '%s\n' "$args" | grep '[d]ockerd'; cat /etc/docker/daemon.json 2>/dev/null); printf '%s\n' "$s" | grep -Eq -e '--authorization-plugin|"authorization-plugins"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*\[[[:space:]]*("|$)' && echo compliant || echo missing

remediation.command: Install an authorization plugin and add it to "authorization-plugins" in /etc/docker/daemon.json (or --authorization-plugin=<PLUGIN>), then restart the Docker daemon.

title: Ensure centralized and remote logging is configured
description: Centralized logging keeps container logs off the host where they can be tampered with. The audit reads the default logging driver from docker info and fails for the local-only drivers json-file, local and none.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 2.14 Ensure centralized and remote logging is configured

audit.command: d=$(docker info --format '{{.LoggingDriver}}') || exit 1; case "$d" in json-file|local|none|'') echo "local:$d";; *) echo compliant;; esac

remediation.command: Set "log-driver" (e.g. syslog, journald forwarded to a collector, fluentd, gelf, splunk) and its "log-opts" in /etc/docker/daemon.json, then restart the Docker daemon.

title: Ensure live restore is enabled for the Docker daemon
description: The live-restore option keeps containers running when the Docker daemon is stopped or restarted.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 2.16 Ensure live restore is enabled

audit.command: docker info --format '{{.LiveRestoreEnabled}}'

remediation.guidance: echo 'Set "live-restore": true in /etc/docker/daemon.json and reload dockerd'

title: Ensure that a daemon-wide custom seccomp profile is applied if appropriate
description: You can choose to apply a custom seccomp profile at a daemon-wide level if needed with this overriding Docker's default seccomp profile. A large number of system calls are exposed to every userland process with many of them not utilized during the entire lifetime of the process. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 2.18 Ensure that a daemon-wide custom seccomp profile is applied if appropriate

audit.command: Docker 22.0 and prior You should run the command below and review the seccomp profile listed in the Security Options section. If it is default this indicates that Docker's default seccomp profile is applied. docker info --format '{{ .SecurityOptions }}' Docker 23 and later The Docker default seccomp profile is reported as profile=builtin, not default.

remediation.command: By default, Docker's default seccomp profile is applied. If this is adequate for your environment, no action is necessary. Alternatively, if you choose to apply your own seccomp profile, use the --seccomp-profile flag at daemon start or put it in the daemon runtime parameters file. dockerd --seccomp-profile </path/to/seccomp/profile>

title: Ensure that experimental features are not implemented in production
description: Experimental features are not stable and should not run in production. The audit reads Server.Experimental from docker version.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 2.19 Ensure that experimental features are not implemented in production

audit.command: docker version --format '{{.Server.Experimental}}'

remediation.guidance: Remove "experimental": true from /etc/docker/daemon.json and --experimental from the dockerd start-up flags, then restart the Docker daemon.

title: Ensure that the daemon.json file ownership is set to root:root
description: /etc/docker/daemon.json must be owned by root:root so that unprivileged users cannot alter Docker behaviour. The audit stats every existing candidate path (/etc/docker/daemon.json); not applicable when none exists.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 3.17 Ensure that the daemon.json file ownership is set to root:root

audit.command: for f in /etc/docker/daemon.json; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; o=$(stat -Lc '%U:%G' "$f") || exit 1; [ "$o" = root:root ] || { echo "$f $o"; exit 0; }; done; echo compliant

remediation.command: for f in /etc/docker/daemon.json; do if [ -e "$f" ]; then chown root:root "$f" || exit 1; fi; done

title: Ensure that daemon.json file permissions are set to 644 or more restrictive
description: /etc/docker/daemon.json must have mode 644 or more restrictive so that it cannot be modified by non-root users. The audit flags any existing candidate path (/etc/docker/daemon.json) with permission bits outside 644; not applicable when none exists.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 3.18 Ensure that daemon.json file permissions are set to 644 or more restrictive

audit.command: for f in /etc/docker/daemon.json; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; out=$(find "$f" -maxdepth 0 -perm /7133) || exit 1; [ -z "$out" ] || { echo "$f"; exit 0; }; done; echo compliant

remediation.command: for f in /etc/docker/daemon.json; do if [ -e "$f" ]; then chmod 644 "$f" || exit 1; fi; done

title: Ensure that the /etc/default/docker file ownership is set to root:root
description: /etc/default/docker (daemon start-up options) must be owned by root:root. The audit stats every existing candidate path (/etc/default/docker); not applicable when none exists.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 3.19 Ensure that the /etc/default/docker file ownership is set to root:root

audit.command: for f in /etc/default/docker; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; o=$(stat -Lc '%U:%G' "$f") || exit 1; [ "$o" = root:root ] || { echo "$f $o"; exit 0; }; done; echo compliant

remediation.command: for f in /etc/default/docker; do if [ -e "$f" ]; then chown root:root "$f" || exit 1; fi; done

title: Ensure that the /etc/default/docker file permissions are set to 644 or more restrictively
description: /etc/default/docker (daemon start-up options) must have mode 644 or more restrictive. The audit flags any existing candidate path (/etc/default/docker) with permission bits outside 644; not applicable when none exists.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 3.20 Ensure that the /etc/default/docker file permissions are set to 644 or more restrictively

audit.command: for f in /etc/default/docker; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; out=$(find "$f" -maxdepth 0 -perm /7133) || exit 1; [ -z "$out" ] || { echo "$f"; exit 0; }; done; echo compliant

remediation.command: for f in /etc/default/docker; do if [ -e "$f" ]; then chmod 644 "$f" || exit 1; fi; done

title: Ensure that the /etc/sysconfig/docker file permissions are set to 644 or more restrictively
description: /etc/sysconfig/docker (daemon start-up options) must have mode 644 or more restrictive. The audit flags any existing candidate path (/etc/sysconfig/docker) with permission bits outside 644; not applicable when none exists.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 3.21 Ensure that the /etc/sysconfig/docker file permissions are set to 644 or more restrictively

audit.command: for f in /etc/sysconfig/docker; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; out=$(find "$f" -maxdepth 0 -perm /7133) || exit 1; [ -z "$out" ] || { echo "$f"; exit 0; }; done; echo compliant

remediation.command: for f in /etc/sysconfig/docker; do if [ -e "$f" ]; then chmod 644 "$f" || exit 1; fi; done

title: Ensure that the /etc/sysconfig/docker file ownership is set to root:root
description: /etc/sysconfig/docker (daemon start-up options) must be owned by root:root. The audit stats every existing candidate path (/etc/sysconfig/docker); not applicable when none exists.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 3.22 Ensure that the /etc/sysconfig/docker file ownership is set to root:root

audit.command: for f in /etc/sysconfig/docker; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; o=$(stat -Lc '%U:%G' "$f") || exit 1; [ "$o" = root:root ] || { echo "$f $o"; exit 0; }; done; echo compliant

remediation.command: for f in /etc/sysconfig/docker; do if [ -e "$f" ]; then chown root:root "$f" || exit 1; fi; done

title: Ensure that a user for the container has been created
description: Containers should run as a non-root user defined in the image (USER) or at run time (--user). Flags containers whose configured user (Config.User) is empty, root or 0; processes that start as root and drop privileges themselves are reported too and need review. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 4.1 Ensure that a user for the container has been created

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} [{{.Config.User}}]' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$2=="[]" || $2 ~ /^\[(root|0)(:.*)?\]$/ {print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Add a USER instruction to the Dockerfile (RUN useradd -r app && ... USER app) or run the container with --user <uid>:<gid>.

title: Ensure that containers use only trusted base images
description: You should ensure that container images you use are either written from scratch or are based on another established and trusted base image downloaded over a secure channel. Official repositories contain Docker images curated and optimized by the Docker community or by their vendor. There is no guarantee that these images are safe and do not contain security vulnerabilities or malicious ... Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 4.2 Ensure that containers use only trusted base images

audit.command: You should review what Docker images are present on the host by executing the command below: docker images This command lists all the container images that are currently available for use on the Docker host. You should then review the origin of each image and review its contents in line with your organization's security policy. You can use the command below to review the history of commits to the image. docker history <imageName>

remediation.command: The following procedures are useful for establishing trust for a specific image. Configure and use Docker Content trust. View the history of each Docker image to evaluate its risk, dependent on the sensitivity of the application you wish to deploy using it. Scan Docker images for vulnerabilities at regular intervals.

title: Ensure that unnecessary packages are not installed in the container
description: Containers should have as small a footprint as possible, and should not contain unnecessary software packages which could increase their attack surface. Unnecessary software should not be installed into containers, as doing so increases their attack surface. Only packages strictly necessary for the correct operation of the application being deployed should be installed. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 4.3 Ensure that unnecessary packages are not installed in the container

audit.command: List all the running instances of containers by executing the command below: docker ps --quiet For each container instance, execute the relevant command for listing all installed packages, e.g.: docker exec $INSTANCE_ID rpm -qa The command above lists the packages installed. You should review the list and ensure that everything installed is actually required.

remediation.command: You should not install anything within the container that is not required. You should consider using a minimal base image rather than the standard CentOS, Debian, or Red Hat images if you can. Some of the options available include BusyBox and Alpine. Not only can this trim your image size considerably, but there would also be fewer pieces of software which could contain vectors for attack.

title: Ensure images are scanned and rebuilt to include security patches
description: Images should be scanned frequently for any vulnerabilities. You should rebuild all images to include these patches and then instantiate new containers from them. Vulnerabilities are loopholes or bugs that can be exploited by hackers or malicious users, and security patches are updates to resolve these vulnerabilities. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 4.4 Ensure images are scanned and rebuilt to include security patches

audit.command: List all the running instances of containers by executing the command below: docker ps --quiet For each container instance, use the package manager within the container (assuming there is one available) to check for the availability of security patches. Alternatively, run image vulnerability assessment tools to scan all the images in your environment.

remediation.command: Images should be re-built ensuring that the latest version of the base images are used, to keep the operating system patch level at an appropriate level. Once the images have been re-built, containers should be re-started making use of the updated images.

title: Ensure update instructions are not used alone in Dockerfiles
description: You should not use OS package manager update instructions such as apt-get update or dnf update either alone or in a single line in any Dockerfiles used to generate images under review. Adding update instructions in a single line on the Dockerfile will cause the update layer to be cached. When you then build any image later using the same instruction, this will cause the previously cached update layer ... Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 4.6 Ensure update instructions are not used alone in Dockerfiles

audit.command: Step 1: Run the command below to get the list of images: docker images Step 2: Run the command below against each image in the list above, looking for any update instructions which are incorporated in a single line: docker history <Image_ID> Alternatively, if you have access to the Dockerfile for the image, you should verify that there are no update instructions configured as described above.

remediation.command: You should use update instructions together with install instructions and version pinning for packages while installing them. This will prevent caching and force the extraction of the required versions. Alternatively, you could use the --no-cache flag during the docker build process to avoid using cached layers.

title: Ensure setuid and setgid permissions are removed
description: Removing setuid and setgid permissions in the images can prevent privilege escalation attacks within containers. setuid and setgid permissions can be used for privilege escalation. Whilst these permissions can on occasion be legitimately needed, you should consider removing them from packages which do not need them. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 4.7 Ensure setuid and setgid permissions are removed

audit.command: You should run the command below against each image to list the executables which have either setuid or setgid permissions: docker export <IMAGE ID> | tar -tv 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^[-rwx].*(s|S).*\s[0-9]' You should then review the list and ensure that all executables configured with these permissions actually require them.

remediation.command: You should allow setuid and setgid permissions only on executables which require them. You could remove these permissions at build time by adding the following command in your Dockerfile, preferably towards the end of the Dockerfile: RUN find / -perm /6000 -type f -exec chmod a-s {} \; || true

title: Ensure that COPY is used instead of ADD in Dockerfiles
description: You should use the COPY instruction instead of the ADD instruction in the Dockerfile. The COPY instruction simply copies files from the local host machine to the container file system. The ADD instruction could potentially retrieve files from remote URLs and perform operations such as unpacking them. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 4.8 Ensure that COPY is used instead of ADD in Dockerfiles

audit.command: Run the command below to get the list of images: docker images Run the command below against each image in the list above and look for any ADD instructions: docker history <IMAGE ID> Alternatively, if you have access to the Dockerfile for the image, you should verify that there are no ADD instructions.

remediation.command: You should use COPY rather than ADD instructions in Dockerfiles.

title: Ensure only verified packages are installed
description: You should verify the authenticity of packages before installing them into images. Verifying authenticity of software packages is essential for building a secure container image. Packages with no known provenance could potentially be malicious or have vulnerabilities that could be exploited. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 4.10 Ensure only verified packages are installed

audit.command: Run the command below to get the list of images: docker images Run the command below for each image in the list above, and check how the authenticity of the packages is being determined. This could be via the use of GPG keys or other secure package distribution mechanisms. docker history <IMAGE ID> Alternatively, if you have access to Dockerfile for the image, verify that the authenticity of the packages is checked.

remediation.command: You should use a secure package distribution mechanism of your choice to ensure the authenticity of software packages.

title: Ensure swarm mode is not Enabled, if not needed
description: Swarm mode opens management ports and a raft store; it should be disabled when the host is not part of a swarm. The audit reads Swarm.LocalNodeState from docker info.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.1 Ensure swarm mode is not Enabled, if not needed

audit.command: docker info --format '{{.Swarm.LocalNodeState}}'

remediation.command: If swarm mode is not needed, leave it with 'docker swarm leave' (managers: --force) after migrating services.

title: Ensure that, if applicable, an AppArmor Profile is enabled
description: AppArmor confines container processes; with AppArmor active on the host every container should run under a profile (docker-default or a custom one). Applies only where AppArmor is enabled (requires /sys/kernel/security/apparmor). Flags containers with an empty or unconfined AppArmorProfile. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.2 Ensure that, if applicable, an AppArmor Profile is enabled

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{.AppArmorProfile}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk 'NF<2 || $2=="unconfined" {print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Run containers with --security-opt apparmor=docker-default (or a custom profile loaded with apparmor_parser) and never apparmor=unconfined.

title: Ensure that, if applicable, SELinux security options are set
description: SELinux labels confine container processes on SELinux hosts. Applies only where SELinux is enabled (requires /sys/fs/selinux/enforce); flags containers without a ProcessLabel (daemon not started with --selinux-enabled, or label=disable). The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.3 Ensure that, if applicable, SELinux security options are set

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{.ProcessLabel}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk 'NF<2 {print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Start dockerd with --selinux-enabled ("selinux-enabled": true in daemon.json) and run containers with appropriate --security-opt label=... options instead of label=disable.

title: Ensure that Linux kernel capabilities are restricted within containers
description: Containers should run with the minimum Linux capabilities; the benchmark specifically asks for NET_RAW to be dropped unless required. Flags containers whose CapDrop contains neither ALL nor NET_RAW (review CapAdd separately). The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.4 Ensure that Linux kernel capabilities are restricted within containers

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{range .HostConfig.CapDrop}}{{.}},{{end}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk 'toupper($0) !~ /(^| |,)(CAP_)?(ALL|NET_RAW),/ {print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Run containers with --cap-drop=ALL (or at least --cap-drop=NET_RAW) and add back only required capabilities with --cap-add.

title: Ensure sshd is not run within containers
description: Running an SSH server inside a container adds attack surface and complicates credential and patch management; use docker exec instead. The audit lists processes of every running container with docker top (no exec into the container) and flags those running sshd.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.7 Ensure sshd is not run within containers

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; bad=''; for i in $ids; do p=$(docker top "$i" -eo comm 2>/dev/null || docker top "$i") || exit 1; printf '%s\n' "$p" | grep -Eq '(^|[ /])sshd( |$)' && bad="$bad $i"; done; [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || echo "sshd running in:$bad"

remediation.command: Remove the SSH server from the image and use docker exec (or an orchestrator equivalent) for administrative access.

title: Ensure privileged ports are not mapped within containers
description: Mapping container ports to host ports below 1024 lets containers occupy ports normally reserved for privileged host services. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.8 Ensure privileged ports are not mapped within containers

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}}{{range $p, $c := .NetworkSettings.Ports}}{{range $c}} {{.HostPort}}{{end}}{{end}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '{for(i=2;i<=NF;i++) if($i+0>0 && $i+0<1024) print $1" "$i}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Republish the container on a host port >= 1024 (docker run -p 8080:80 ...) and remove privileged port mappings from compose files.

title: Ensure that only needed ports are open on the container
description: The Dockerfile for a container image defines the ports which are opened by default on a container instance. The list of ports are relevant to the application you are running within the container and should only be open if they are needed. A container can be run with only the ports defined in the Dockerfile for its image or can alternatively be arbitrarily passed run time parameters to open a list of ports. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.9 Ensure that only needed ports are open on the container

audit.command: You should list all the running instances of containers and their associated port mappings by executing the command below: docker ps --quiet | xargs docker inspect --format '{{ .Id }}: Ports={{ .NetworkSettings.Ports }}' You should then review the list and ensure that all the ports mapped are in fact genuinely required by each container.

remediation.command: You should ensure that the Dockerfile for each container image only exposes needed ports. You can also completely ignore the list of ports defined in the Dockerfile by NOT using -P (UPPERCASE) or the --publish-all flag when starting the container. Instead, use the -p (lowercase) or --publish flag to explicitly define the ports that you need for a particular container instance. For example: docker run --interactive --tty --publish 5000 --publish 5001 --publish 5002 centos /bin/bash

title: Ensure that the memory usage for containers is limited
description: Without a memory limit a single container can exhaust host memory (denial of service). Flags containers with HostConfig.Memory = 0. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.11 Ensure that the memory usage for containers is limited

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{.HostConfig.Memory}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$2=="0"{print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Redeploy with a memory limit (docker run --memory=512m ...; compose: deploy.resources.limits.memory / mem_limit).

title: Ensure that CPU priority is set appropriately on containers
description: By default, all containers on a Docker host share resources equally. By using the resource management capabilities of the Docker host you can control the host CPU resources that a container may consume. By default, CPU time is divided between containers equally. If you wish to control available CPU resources amongst container instances, you can use the CPU sharing feature. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.12 Ensure that CPU priority is set appropriately on containers

audit.command: You should run the following command: docker ps --quiet --all | xargs docker inspect --format '{{ .Id }}: CpuShares={{ .HostConfig.CpuShares }}' If the above command returns 0 or 1024, it means that CPU shares are not in place. If it returns a non-zero value other than 1024, it means that they are in place.

remediation.command: You should manage the CPU runtime between your containers dependent on their priority within your organization. To do so start the container using the --cpu-shares argument. For example, you could run a container as below: docker run -d --cpu-shares 512 centos sleep 1000 In the example above, the container is started with CPU shares of 50% of what other containers use. So if the other container has CPU shares of 80%, this container will have CPU shares of 40%. Every new container will have 1024 shares of CPU by default.

title: Ensure that the container's root filesystem is mounted as read only
description: A read-only root filesystem stops attackers from modifying the container's binaries and configuration at runtime. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.13 Ensure that the container's root filesystem is mounted as read only

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{.HostConfig.ReadonlyRootfs}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$2!="true"{print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Redeploy with --read-only (compose: 'read_only: true') and use volumes or --tmpfs for directories that must be writable.

title: Ensure that incoming container traffic is bound to a specific host interface
description: Ports published without a host IP listen on all interfaces (0.0.0.0 / ::), exposing the service on every network the host is attached to. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.14 Ensure that incoming container traffic is bound to a specific host interface

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}}{{range $p, $c := .NetworkSettings.Ports}}{{range $c}} [{{.HostIp}}]{{end}}{{end}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '{for(i=2;i<=NF;i++) if($i=="[]" || $i=="[0.0.0.0]" || $i=="[::]") {print $1; break}}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Republish the container bound to a specific interface, e.g. docker run -p 10.2.3.4:49153:80 ... (compose: "10.2.3.4:49153:80").

title: Ensure that host devices are not directly exposed to containers
description: Host devices passed with --device give the container direct access to hardware, bypassing isolation. Flags containers with any HostConfig.Devices entry. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.18 Ensure that host devices are not directly exposed to containers

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{len .HostConfig.Devices}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$2+0>0{print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Redeploy without --device unless strictly required; if required, grant the minimum permissions (e.g. --device=/dev/xyz:/dev/xyz:r).

title: Ensure that the default ulimit is overwritten at runtime if needed
description: The default ulimit is set at the Docker daemon level. However, if you need to, you may override the default ulimit setting during container runtime. ulimit provides control over the resources available to the shell and to processes started by it. Setting system resource limits in a prudent fashion, protects against denial of service conditions. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.19 Ensure that the default ulimit is overwritten at runtime if needed

audit.command: You should run the command below: docker ps --quiet --all | xargs docker inspect --format '{{ .Id }}: Ulimits={{ .HostConfig.Ulimits }}' This command should return Ulimits=<no value> for each container instance unless there is a need in a specific case to override the default settings.

remediation.command: You should only override the default ulimit settings if needed in a specific case. For example, to override default ulimit settings start a container as below: docker run -ti -d --ulimit nofile=1024:1024 centos sleep 1000

title: Ensure mount propagation mode is not set to shared
description: A shared (or rshared) mount propagates mount changes between the container and the host. Flags containers with any mount whose Propagation is shared or rshared. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.20 Ensure mount propagation mode is not set to shared

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}}{{range .Mounts}} {{.Propagation}}{{end}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '/ r?shared( |$)/ {print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Redeploy without :shared/:rshared bind-mount propagation (use the default rprivate, or slave if required).

title: Ensure that the host's UTS namespace is not shared
description: Sharing the host's UTS namespace allows the container to change the host's hostname. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.21 Ensure that the host's UTS namespace is not shared

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{.HostConfig.UTSMode}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$2=="host"{print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Redeploy without --uts=host (compose: remove 'uts: host').

title: Ensure that Docker commands always make use of the latest version of their image
description: You should always ensure that you are using the latest version of the images within your repository and not cached older versions. Multiple Docker commands such as docker pull, docker run etc. are known to have an issue where by default, they extract the local copy of the image, if present, even though there is an updated version of the image with ... Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.28 Ensure that Docker commands always make use of the latest version of their image

audit.command: You should carry out the following steps: Step 1: Open your image repository and list the image version history for the image you are inspecting. Step 2: Observe the status when the docker pull command is triggered. If the status is shown as Image is up to date, it means that you are getting the cached version of the image. Step 3: Match the version of the image you are running to the latest version reported in your repository and this will tell you whether you are running the cached version or the latest copy.

remediation.command: You should use proper version pinning mechanisms (the "latest" tag which is assigned by default is still vulnerable to caching attacks) to avoid extracting cached older versions. Version pinning mechanisms should be used for base images, packages, and entire images. You can customize version pinning rules according to your requirements.

title: Ensure that the PIDs cgroup limit is used
description: Without a PIDs cgroup limit a fork bomb in one container can exhaust host process slots. Flags containers whose PidsLimit is unset, 0 or -1. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.29 Ensure that the PIDs cgroup limit is used

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{.HostConfig.PidsLimit}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$2=="<nil>" || $2=="0" || $2=="-1"{print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Redeploy with --pids-limit (e.g. --pids-limit=100; compose: 'pids_limit: 100') or set "default-pids-limit" in daemon.json.

title: Ensure that the host's user namespaces are not shared
description: UsernsMode=host disables user namespace remapping for the container, so root in the container is root on the host. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.31 Ensure that the host's user namespaces are not shared

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{.HostConfig.UsernsMode}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$2=="host"{print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Redeploy without --userns=host (compose: remove 'userns_mode: host').

title: Ensure that the minimum number of manager nodes have been created in a swarm
description: You should ensure that the minimum number of required manager nodes is created in a swarm. Manager nodes within a swarm have control over the swarm and can change its configuration, including modifying security parameters. Having excessive manager nodes could render the swarm more susceptible to compromise. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 7.1 Ensure that the minimum number of manager nodes have been created in a swarm

audit.command: Run docker info and verify the number of managers. docker info --format '{{ .Swarm.Managers }}' Alternatively run the below command. docker node ls | grep 'Leader' Expected state: If an excessive number of managers is configured, the excess nodes can be demoted to workers using the following command: docker node demote <ID> Where <ID> is the node ID value of the manager to be demoted.

remediation.command: If an excessive number of managers is configured, the excess nodes can be demoted to workers using the following command: docker node demote <ID> Where <ID> is the node ID value of the manager to be demoted.

title: Ensure that swarm services are bound to a specific host interface
description: By default, Docker swarm services will listen on all interfaces on the host. This may not be necessary for the operation of the swarm where the host has multiple network interfaces. When a swarm is initialized the default value for the --listen-addr flag is 0.0.0.0:2377 which means that swarm services will listen on all interfaces on the host. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 7.2 Ensure that swarm services are bound to a specific host interface

audit.command: You should check the network listener on port 2377 (the default for docker swarm) and 7946 (container network discovery), and confirm that it is only listening on specific interfaces. For example, in this could be done using the following command: ss -lp | grep -iE ':2377|:7946'

remediation.command: Resolving this issues requires re-initialization of the swarm, specifying a specific interface for the --listen-addr parameter.

title: Ensure that all Docker swarm overlay networks are encrypted
description: Overlay network traffic between swarm nodes is unencrypted by default. On an active swarm node every overlay network must have the encrypted option; compliant when swarm mode is inactive.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 7.3 Ensure that all Docker swarm overlay networks are encrypted

audit.command: st=$(docker info --format '{{.Swarm.LocalNodeState}}') || exit 1; [ "$st" = active ] || { echo compliant; exit 0; }; ns=$(docker network ls --filter driver=overlay --quiet) || exit 1; [ -z "$ns" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker network inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{index .Options "encrypted"}}' $ns) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk 'NF<2 {print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf 'unencrypted overlay: %s\n' $bad

remediation.command: Create overlay networks with --opt encrypted (docker network create -d overlay --opt encrypted <name>) and move services onto them.

title: Ensure that swarm manager is run in auto-lock mode
description: Auto-lock protects the swarm raft keys at rest so a stolen manager disk cannot be used without the unlock key. On an active swarm manager the cluster spec must have AutoLockManagers true; compliant on non-swarm hosts and workers.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 7.5 Ensure that swarm manager is run in auto-lock mode

audit.command: st=$(docker info --format '{{.Swarm.LocalNodeState}}') || exit 1; [ "$st" = active ] || { echo compliant; exit 0; }; m=$(docker info --format '{{.Swarm.ControlAvailable}}') || exit 1; [ "$m" = true ] || { echo compliant; exit 0; }; v=$(docker info --format '{{.Swarm.Cluster.Spec.EncryptionConfig.AutoLockManagers}}') || exit 1; [ "$v" = true ] && echo compliant || echo "autolock $v"

remediation.command: docker swarm update --autolock=true on a manager and store the unlock key securely.

title: Ensure that node certificates are rotated as appropriate
description: You should rotate swarm node certificates in line with your organizational security policy. Docker Swarm uses TLS for clustering operations between its nodes. Certificate rotation ensures that in an event such as a compromised node or key, it is difficult to impersonate a node. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 7.7 Ensure that node certificates are rotated as appropriate

audit.command: Run one of the commands below and ensure that the node certificate Expiry Duration is set as appropriate. docker info | grep "Expiry Duration" docker info --format 'NodeCertExpiry: {{ .Swarm.Cluster.Spec.CAConfig.NodeCertExpiry }}'

remediation.command: You should run the command to set the desired expiry time on the node certificate. For example: docker swarm update --cert-expiry 48h

title: Ensure that CA certificates are rotated as appropriate
description: You should rotate root CA certificates as appropriate. Docker Swarm uses TLS for clustering operations between its nodes. Certificate rotation ensures that in an event such as a compromised node or key, it is difficult to impersonate a node. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 7.8 Ensure that CA certificates are rotated as appropriate

audit.command: You should check the time stamp on the root CA certificate file. For example: ls -l /var/lib/docker/swarm/certificates/swarm-root-ca.crt The certificate should show a time stamp in line with the organizational rotation policy.

remediation.command: You should run the command below to rotate a certificate. docker swarm ca --rotate

title: Ensure that management plane traffic is separated from data plane traffic
description: 9/30/26 1.9.0 Included support for Docker V29.x 9/30/26 1.9.0 Edited grammar and typos in recommendation 1.1.13 Ticket #28427 9/30/26 1.9.0 Updated syntax in recommendation 1.1.5 Ticket #28426 9/30/26 1.9.0 Edit command usage in recommendation 7.9 Ticket #28425 9/30/26 1.9.0 Updates service name in recommendation 3.24 ... Separating management plane traffic from data plane traffic ensures that these types of traffic are segregated from each other. These traffic flows can then be individually monitored and tied to different traffic ... Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 7.9 Ensure that management plane traffic is separated from data plane traffic

audit.command: You should run the command below on each swarm node and ensure that the management plane address is different from the data plane address. docker info --format 'Swarm Node Address: {{.Swarm.NodeAddr}}' Expected state: You should initialize the swarm with dedicated interfaces for management and data planes respectively. For example: docker swarm init --advertise-addr=192.168.0.1 --data-path-addr=17.1.0.3

remediation.command: You should initialize the swarm with dedicated interfaces for management and data planes respectively. For example: docker swarm init --advertise-addr=192.168.0.1 --data-path-addr=17.1.0.3

title: Ensure the logging level is set to 'info'
description: The info log level captures all logs except debug; lower levels lose security events and debug floods logs. Compliant when log-level is unset (default info) or set to info. The audit reads the running dockerd command line (ps) together with /etc/docker/daemon.json.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 2.3 Ensure the logging level is set to 'info'

audit.command: args=$(ps -eo args 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; s=$(printf '%s\n' "$args" | grep '[d]ockerd'; cat /etc/docker/daemon.json 2>/dev/null); printf '%s\n' "$s" | grep -Eq -e '(--log-level[= ]+|"log-level"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*")(debug|warn|error|fatal)' && echo noncompliant || echo compliant

remediation.guidance: Remove the log-level option or set "log-level": "info" in /etc/docker/daemon.json (remove --log-level from the dockerd start-up flags) and restart the Docker daemon.

title: Ensure base device size is not changed until needed
description: Increasing the base device size (dm.basesize) can affect all images and containers and should only be done when needed. Compliant when no dm.basesize storage option is set on the dockerd command line or in /etc/docker/daemon.json.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 2.12 Ensure base device size is not changed until needed

audit.command: args=$(ps -eo args 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; s=$(printf '%s\n' "$args" | grep '[d]ockerd'; cat /etc/docker/daemon.json 2>/dev/null); printf '%s\n' "$s" | grep -q 'dm\.basesize' && echo noncompliant || echo compliant

remediation.guidance: Remove dm.basesize from "storage-opts" in /etc/docker/daemon.json and from --storage-opt start-up flags unless it is genuinely needed, then restart the Docker daemon.

title: Ensure Userland Proxy is Disabled
description: The userland proxy (docker-proxy) adds attack surface; hairpin NAT through iptables is preferred. Compliant when userland-proxy is set to false. The audit reads the running dockerd command line (ps) together with /etc/docker/daemon.json.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 2.17 Ensure Userland Proxy is Disabled

audit.command: args=$(ps -eo args 2>/dev/null) || exit 1; s=$(printf '%s\n' "$args" | grep '[d]ockerd'; cat /etc/docker/daemon.json 2>/dev/null); printf '%s\n' "$s" | grep -Eq -e '--userland-proxy[= ]+false|"userland-proxy"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*false' && echo compliant || echo missing

remediation.guidance: Set "userland-proxy": false in /etc/docker/daemon.json and restart the Docker daemon.

title: Ensure that HEALTHCHECK instructions have been added to container images
description: A HEALTHCHECK lets the engine detect and report unhealthy containers. Flags running containers whose configuration (inherited from the image) has no healthcheck. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 4.5 Ensure that HEALTHCHECK instructions have been added to container images

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}}{{if .Config.Healthcheck}} yes{{end}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk 'NF<2 {print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Add a HEALTHCHECK instruction to the Dockerfile (or --health-cmd at run time) and rebuild the image.

title: Ensure that the 'on-failure' container restart policy is set to '5'
description: Restart policy 'always' (or on-failure with unlimited retries) can hide failures and turn a crashing container into a resource drain; on-failure with at most 5 retries is recommended. Flags always, unless-stopped and on-failure with 0 or more than 5 retries. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.15 Ensure that the 'on-failure' container restart policy is set to '5'

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{.HostConfig.RestartPolicy.Name}} {{.HostConfig.RestartPolicy.MaximumRetryCount}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$2=="always" || $2=="unless-stopped" || ($2=="on-failure" && ($3+0==0 || $3+0>5)){print $1" "$2":"$3}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Redeploy with --restart=on-failure:5 (compose: 'restart: on-failure:5') or update in place: docker update --restart=on-failure:5 <container>.

title: Ensure that cgroup usage is confirmed
description: Containers should run in the default Docker cgroup unless a specific, controlled parent cgroup is intended. Flags containers with a non-empty HostConfig.CgroupParent for review. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.25 Ensure that cgroup usage is confirmed

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} [{{.HostConfig.CgroupParent}}]' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '$2!="[]" {print $1" "$2}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Run containers without --cgroup-parent unless a specific, reviewed cgroup is required.

title: Ensure that container health is checked at runtime
description: The container health status must be checked at runtime. Flags running containers that report no health status (no healthcheck configured). The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.27 Ensure that container health is checked at runtime

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}}{{if .State.Health}} {{.State.Health.Status}}{{end}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk 'NF<2 {print $1}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Configure a healthcheck (HEALTHCHECK in the image or --health-cmd at run time) and monitor docker inspect .State.Health.Status.

title: Ensure that Docker's default bridge "docker0" is not used
description: Containers on the default bridge (docker0) can reach each other without restriction and are exposed to ARP spoofing; user-defined networks should be used. Flags containers attached to the network named bridge. The audit inspects every running container (docker ps -q) and prints the offending names; a host with no running containers is compliant.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 5.30 Ensure that Docker's default bridge "docker0" is not used

audit.command: ids=$(docker ps -q) || exit 1; [ -z "$ids" ] && { echo compliant; exit 0; }; out=$(docker inspect --format '{{.Name}}{{range $n, $_ := .NetworkSettings.Networks}} {{$n}}{{end}}' $ids) || exit 1; bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | awk '{for(i=2;i<=NF;i++) if($i=="bridge") {print $1; break}}'); [ -z "$bad" ] && echo compliant || printf '%s\n' "$bad"

remediation.command: Create user-defined networks (docker network create ...) and attach containers to them instead of the default bridge.

title: Ensure that image sprawl is avoided
description: You should not keep a large number of container images on the same host. Use only tagged images as appropriate. Tagged images are useful if you need to fall back from the "latest" version to a specific version of an image in production. Images with unused or old tags may contain vulnerabilities that might be exploited if ... Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 6.1 Ensure that image sprawl is avoided

audit.command: Step 1 Make a list of all image IDs that are currently instantiated by executing the command below: docker images --quiet | xargs docker inspect --format '{{ .Id }}: Image={{ .Config.Image }}' Step 2: List all the images present on the system by executing the command below: docker images Step 3: Compare the list of image IDs from Step 1 and Step 2 and look for images that are currently not in use. If any unused or old images are found, discuss with the system administrator the need to keep such images on the system. If images are no longer needed they should be deleted.

remediation.command: You should keep only the images that you actually need and establish a workflow to remove old or stale images from the host. Additionally, you should use features such as pull-by-digest to get specific images from the registry. You can follow the steps below to find unused images on the system so they can be deleted. Step 1 Make a list of all image IDs that are currently instantiated by executing the command below: docker images --quiet | xargs docker inspect --format '{{ .Id }}: Image={{ .Config.Image }}' Step 2: List all the images present on the system by executing the command below ...

title: Ensure that container sprawl is avoided
description: Large numbers of stopped containers waste resources and hide stale, unpatched workloads. Whether the count is excessive is a site decision, so this is a manual review.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 6.2 Ensure that container sprawl is avoided

audit.command: Review container sprawl: compare docker info --format '{{ .ContainersStopped }}' with docker info --format '{{ .ContainersRunning }}', list stopped containers with docker ps -a --filter status=exited and remove the ones no longer needed.

remediation.command: Remove unused containers: docker container prune (or docker rm <id> for specific containers) after confirming they are not needed.

title: Ensure that the swarm manager auto-lock key is rotated periodically
description: You should rotate the swarm manager auto-lock key periodically. The swarm manager auto-lock key is not automatically rotated. Good security practice is to rotate keys. Reported as a manual review item: the audit needs a site-specific judgement.
reference: CIS Docker Benchmark v1.9.0 - 7.6 Ensure that the swarm manager auto-lock key is rotated periodically

audit.command: Currently, there is no mechanism to find out when the key was last rotated on a swarm manager node. You should check with the system administrator to see if there is a key rotation process, and how often the key is rotated.

remediation.command: You should run the command below to rotate the keys: docker swarm unlock-key --rotate Additionally, to facilitate auditing of this recommendation, you should maintain key rotation records and ensure that you establish a pre-defined frequency for key rotation.
